content:
Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Yearlong Planning Overview and Caution

In Episode 9, we explored a four-step process for planning a SINGLE unit. And after hearing that, it's natural to start wondering how to plan a yearlong writing curriculum, so we'll address that now in Episode 10.

But before we dive in, a word of caution: As much as we love a plan, a pacing guide, a scope and sequence — I encourage you NOT to rush into this the first year of a focused writing initiative. A curriculum map isn't helpful if you don't have 1) regular time set aside for writing, 2) a clear understanding of effective mini-lesson instruction, or 3) a grade-level sequence of essential skills to teach within each mode. THESE are the top 3 priorities. Think of this as WHEN you'll teach, HOW you'll teach, and WHAT you'll teach. Give yourself time to master these foundational pieces!

Consequently, for the first year or more — stick with your EXISTING curriculum map, your PREVIOUS scope and sequence, or whatever framework has guided your writing instruction in the past. Be mindful of YOUR OWN cognitive load and give yourself grace and time to master these three priorities before adding more.

That all said, some of you will view this episode to capture the vision of what's ahead, while others ARE ready to move forward and learn the facets and factors to create a yearlong writing plan.

section_name: Plan Instruction for 3 Areas of Writing
content:
Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Plan Instruction for 3 Areas of Writing

The science behind teaching writing effectively is clear: students require direct instruction and ample practice time in three key areas: 1) how to Apply LANGUAGE FOUNDATIONS, 2) how to EXPRESS IDEAS for different purposes, and 3) how to demonstrate comprehension in writing.

Acknowledging these 3 areas of writing instruction also accounts for the components found on state testing rubrics. Most standardized reading tests require intermediate students to 3) write about texts to show comprehension, 2) BY composing a persuasive, informative, or narrative response, 1) while demonstrating a strong command of language conventions.

Consequently, the state test isn't something we cram for — it measures skills taught across the year. Its rigor comes from integrating all three facets of writing into a single, complex task that students must complete independently, and often in one sitting. Therefore, a strong yearlong writing curriculum must intentionally address the instruction and practice of all three areas.

For the K-2 teachers viewing this episode, this 3-pronged writing instruction applies to your young learners, too! While their writing products may look different (perhaps a labeled picture or a simple sentence), each of these THREE writing components is ALSO an expectation within your grade-level standards. In fact, your direct instruction in kindergarten, first, and second grade lays the foundation for success on state assessments!

Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Three Distinct Scope and Sequences

Given the complexity of learning how to write and the 3 areas of instruction we must provide, we need to have THREE distinct scope and sequences. Although this mini series has predominantly focused on how to teach the writing modes, let me briefly address what curriculum maps look like for the other two areas.

LANGUAGE FOUNDATIONS form the bedrock of writing fluency, which is why most primary teachers use resources to address print concepts, letter formation, spelling, encoding, and sentence construction. This focus on conventions CONTINUES through the upper grades, with added attention to grammar, mechanics, and other transcription skills. If you're following a language foundation program, you're likely providing the systematic instruction needed for this crucial aspect of learning to write.

In addition to language foundations, READING RESPONSE skills also require systematic instruction. In the intermediate grades, this includes teaching students how to take notes or annotate, write story summaries, recall facts or summarize information, support answers with evidence in short written responses, AND how to pull information from one or more texts in order to produce multi-paragraph compositions.

Now, the challenge isn't assigning these bigger read-write tasks, but providing the direct instruction they require. Without mini-lessons on how to WRITE these responses, students will struggle to do them independently. This is where a second curriculum map is needed — one that outlines the writing skills to TEACH and practice within the reading block.

Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Teach the 3 Writing Modes

With a general understanding of the skills involved in reading responses and language foundations, it becomes clear what's missing: instruction on the three writing modes.

Students can't INDEPENDENTLY write a persuasive about animals in cages at the zoo if they haven't learned how to organize persuasive writing as WHAT I think / WHY I think it. Primary students can't INDEPENDENTLY draw and label a picture to explain a new science concept if they haven't learned how to communicate information through pictorial writing. Intermediate students can't INDEPENDENTLY write a fictional story based on facts gleaned from a nonfiction text if they haven't been taught HOW all narratives are structured around a problem and its solution.

THE POINT: Students can't write a persuasive, informative, OR narrative READING response if they don't know how to WRITE in that mode. That's the critical third area of instruction we must provide.

Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Spiraled Instruction Through Mini-Units

Creating a scope and sequence for writing genres tends to be much more difficult. This may be in part because there is NO definitive research on the BEST ORDER to teach writing units. HOWEVER, there IS abundant research that CLEARLY demonstrates the value of spiraling your genre instruction. Let's look at what the experts have discovered and then apply it to our planning process.

John Hattie's (2009) meta-analysis highlights the power of CUMULATIVE practice and ONGOING review to BUILD writing abilities. And Doug Fisher (2010) emphasizes the importance of "accumulated writing capital," emphasizing that writing development is A GRADUAL, CUMULATIVE process.

On the surface it seems that we should revisit writing skills and genres throughout the year, which I'm supposing most teachers already do. And while that IS part of what the research states, the more important facet is the emphasis on spiraling our INSTRUCTION.

Rather than teaching ALL of the writing skills in a single unit, the science recommends that we design a writing curriculum made up of MINI units.

section_name: Mini-Unit Structure and Layered Skill Building
content:
Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Mini-Unit Structure and Layered Skill Building

For example, in the first mini unit, we may only teach one or two writing skills. These would be essential skills that are foundational to that writing mode. The mini unit might only last one or two weeks and end with students generating a short first-draft-only that is assessed for just those two skills AND the application of all language foundations previously taught.

Then a couple weeks later, the same writing mode appears on the curriculum map. This second mini unit begins by reviewing the writing purpose AND the first two skills previously taught. This reinforces to students that those ingredients are essential to this mode of writing. Then the mini unit continues and introduces a third NEW skill during mini lesson instruction. Again, this mini unit ends with students producing another NEW writing.

This is NOT the same piece that they created at the end of unit one, and as we learned in Ep 9, this is not the same writing they would have been working on DURING this mini unit. Instead, it's on a brand new topic where students are to integrate the first two skills AND the most recent skill ALONG with applying all known language conventions taught to this point.

This process would continue with a third and possibly fourth mini unit, reviewing what was previously learned and adding one or two more skills.

This continues throughout the year where by the end, students will have been taught all of the same skills as in a traditional, mono unit, but the mini-unit approach LAYERED the instruction, honoring the researched best practice of "accumulating writing capital." It allows students time to practice, grow, and develop their genre-writing skills at a manageable pace — versus the mono unit where students were expected to learn everything at once AND apply it ALL immediately.

Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Spiraling Modes and Primary/ML Considerations

In between mini units on one mode of writing, execute parallel mini units on the other two modes. Teach the unique purposes, key ingredients, and text structures of EACH type of writing. As students cycle through the modes, they have a second, third, and fourth chance to learn and experience what goes into that type of writing. THIS is why spiraled instruction works! As the year progresses, skills accumulate, students gain automaticity, and their confidence grows.

Now, let's take this mini-unit concept and apply it to the primary grade levels, or those who work with Multilingual learners at levels 1 and 2. This mini unit approach applies to you too, as you're ALSO charged with teaching students the essential ingredients of persuasive, informative, and narrative writing.

The difference is that your students will express their ideas within their developmental writing stage — meaning they will integrate the essential ingredients within pictures, labels, and listed words, before they do it in complete sentences. But as we have learned in previous episodes, we DON'T have to wait until students are all writing sentences to TEACH them the essential ingredients and structures of the 3 writing modes.

All grade levels have standards that direct us to EACH deliver instruction in 3 areas — language foundations, reading responses, AND writing modes.

Primary, Special Ed, and ML teachers should note that as students' language foundations improve, they may be at a different developmental stage when the mode reappears in a future mini-unit. This emphasizes the need to review prior skills at the start of each mini-unit, reminding students of what they've learned AND modeling how to apply it to the new stage or writing template.

section_name: General Knowledge Writing Topics and Testing Prep
content:
Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — General Knowledge Writing Topics and Testing Prep

One last note for teachers in testing grades: Look at the month leading up to the state assessment. A mini-unit calendar allows for authentic review of all three writing modes — ensuring YOUR students are prepared for any prompt they may encounter.

Now let's address the TOPICS students will write about within these mini-units.

In Episode 9, I highlighted the value of general knowledge or school-based topics to practice NEW writing skills DURING a unit. I recommend EXTENDING THIS to include the topics for students' end-of-unit products as well.

Consider having students write ONLY about general knowledge topics for ALL genre writing experiences in FIRST SEMESTER. I suggest this based on 3 factors:

1) Cognitive load: As I mentioned in Ep 9, when students write about unfamiliar topics, they're balancing limited background knowledge with a new writing SKILL. Well, this same thinking applies when trying a new writing MODE, as well. If a student's end-of-unit product is weak, it's hard to tell if the struggle is with the mode itself or the topic.

2) Stamina building: While teaching writing skills, we must also build students' stamina as writers. Strong writing isn't just about skills — it's about sustaining effort. Students need to gradually write more words, sentences, paragraphs, and pages — and familiar topics help them persevere and build endurance.

3) More writing, more practice: If writing DOESN'T depend on prior reading, we can do it more often — leading to more practice and faster skill development.

section_name: Merging All 3 Areas in Second Semester
content:
Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Merging All 3 Areas in Second Semester

Now, EVEN IF you're assigning general knowledge topics for BOTH the during-unit practice AND end-of-unit assessment, KNOW that your students ARE still learning and practicing how to write about texts. They are experiencing it within the READING block. During first semester, students are learning to apply known language conventions WHILE taking notes, writing simple summaries, and generating short constructed responses.

My recommendations aside, you CAN assign texts and content to be the topics for end-of-unit products — EVEN in first semester. Just be cautious about doing this too soon. Early on, the first mini units are laying the foundation for essential MODE-specific WRITING skills. Consequently, IF you assign an end-of-unit product on a content-area concept within the first semester, choose something well-known — something students have studied in depth.

Now, it's time to merge the GENRE-INSTRUCTIONAL map with READING response skills and LANGUAGE foundations.

By second semester, students have built a strong foundation in each writing mode AND developed stamina as writers. The focus now shifts from HOW to write in a genre to APPLYING its key ingredients to more complex topics and texts.

section_name: Second Semester Reading-Response and Genre Integration
content:
Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Second Semester Reading-Response and Genre Integration

In the first semester, INTERMEDIATE students practiced writing about a single text and crafting one-paragraph responses. Now, in the second semester, reading-response skills advance. The focus shifts from analyzing one text to comparing and synthesizing ideas from multiple sources. However, consuming more texts and LONGER texts will take up MORE time in the reading block, making it even harder to allocate time for write-about-reading instruction. THIS is normal.

And it's WHY the second semester of GENRE instruction is where all future write-about-reading skills are taught. These intermediate mini-lessons may include: decoding a prompt to determine the writing mode; organizing and citing evidence from multiple sources; expanding inferences, syntheses, or main ideas into topic sentences and text evidence; stacking multiple paragraphs to create longer informative or persuasive responses; planning original narratives using facts from nonfiction texts; and rewriting short stories from different characters' points of view.

Teaching these new READING-response skills will occur within GENRE-instruction mini-lessons. Likewise, the WRITING TIME will no longer revolve around general knowledge topics. Everything taught and practiced within genre-instruction NOW centers on responding to texts.

Here's the BIG PICTURE — The skills built during FIRST-semester reading and genre instruction directly fuel students' ability to craft longer, more developed responses in the second semester.

Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Primary Grades Second Semester Progression

A similar progression happens in the primary grades. The reading responses generated during first semester were likely LIMITED by students' developing language skills. Many may have expressed comprehension through pictures and labels OR even relied on whole-class writing with the teacher scribing.

However, in second semester, the growing language foundations allows for a shift in the writing products. The reading-response tasks that WERE whole-class activities are apt to become independent tasks. Likewise, as mini-units continue in genre-writing, students apply growing language foundations as they express their own ideas about TEXTS and subject-area TOPICS in their end-of-unit products.

section_name: Prioritize Essential Skills, First Drafts, and Embrace Variety
content:
Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Prioritize Essential Skills, First Drafts, and Embrace Variety

With this yearlong vision in mind, let's now focus on the smaller components that shape a curriculum map of mini-units.

Prioritize the essential skills: In previous episodes, we reviewed grade-level writing standards and identified four essential skills that define the core elements and structure of each writing mode. These skills should be taught early, in the first rounds of mini-units. They are foundational because they focus on the TYPE of information each mode utilizes and its overall STRUCTURE. While the other skills listed within your grade-level standards are relevant, TEACH them in mini-units executed later in the year.

Adjust for the writing process: Mini-units focus more on first drafts than final drafts — and that's intentional. While you CAN extend any mini-unit for revising, editing, and publishing time, I believe students should only take a few pieces through the final draft process. Here's why: Since state assessments only allow time for first drafts, students need to have frequent experience with one-and-done writings. Primary writers often struggle to reread their work, so starting fresh each day makes a lot of sense! Subject-area and real-world writing often stops at a first draft, requiring initial drafts to be strong and cohesive. That doesn't mean we AREN'T using the writing process within mini-units. It's just more condensed. We need to teach writers how to ADAPT the process to fit the task and timeframe. And teaching this is recognized within the standards that reference providing FREQUENT short experiences and OCCASIONAL longer ones.

Embrace the variety: Frequent mode-switching may seem confusing, but science supports it. Leading researcher Steve Graham emphasizes that EFFECTIVE INSTRUCTION helps students grasp each genre's goals and ADAPT to different contexts and audiences. By starting each mini unit with a REVIEW of its known ingredients — compared to the other 2 modes — we are building stronger writers. In fact, this ability to adjust for different writing purposes is so vital that state tests often code a student's writing as UNSCOREABLE if it doesn't utilize the genre and structure specified in the prompt.

Episode 10 Elementary: Mini-Units — Key Takeaways

As I wrap up this video, let me identify 2 important takeaways.

Number 1: Don't rush to build a yearlong curriculum map. This IS a step you'll want to take, but managing writing time and delivering dynamic direct instruction are the first priorities.

Number 2: With SOOO many factors going into planning a yearlong writing curriculum, recognize that it'll be a working document under revision for several years. This is NOT something that is built in a couple meetings over the summer.

That said, before focusing on building a curriculum map, I encourage you to assess these three priorities: 1) Is there dedicated time for genre writing? 2) Are mini-lessons being delivered? 3) Is there a clear sequence of grade-level skills per mode? By doing this, we take the next step toward building better writers.
